title: Supply of coffee
questionText: Suppose that the price of coffee increases from $6 per kg to $8 per kg. What should happen to supply?
answers: There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be a decrease in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
explanation: A change in the good's own price moves us along the supply curve. A higher price makes production more profitable, so quantity supplied rises — an expansion.

title: Supply of wheat
questionText: Consider the supply of wheat. Suppose the price of wheat rises from $3 to $5 per kg. What happens to the supply of wheat?
answers: There will be an increase in supply, from 75 to 125 tonnes
There will be a contraction in supply, from 125 to 75 tonnes
There will be an expansion in supply, from 75 to 125 tonnes
There will be a decrease in supply, from 125 to 75 tonnes
explanation: A higher own price is a movement along the supply curve. Producers offer more — an expansion — from 75 to 125 tonnes.

title: Supply of wheat
questionText: Wheat and rice are related goods that can be substituted in production. The price of rice falls on global markets, shifting the supply of wheat from S1 to S2. At a price of $3 per kg, what has happened to the supply of wheat?
answers: An increase in supply, from 75 to 125 tonnes
An expansion in supply, from 75 to 125 tonnes
A decrease in supply, from 125 to 75 tonnes
A contraction in supply, from 125 to 75 tonnes
explanation: Wheat and rice are substitutes in production. Cheaper rice makes wheat relatively more attractive to grow, so the whole wheat supply curve shifts right — an increase from 75 to 125 tonnes.

questionText: Which of the following would cause a movement along the supply curve for wheat, rather than a shift of the whole curve?
answers: A fall in the price of the fertiliser used to grow wheat
An improvement in harvesting technology
A government subsidy paid to wheat farmers
A rise in the price of wheat
explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves us along the supply curve. Cheaper fertiliser, better technology and subsidies all shift the whole curve.

title: Supply of manufactured goods
questionText: An increase in the minimum wage for a manufacturing firm raises the cost of labour for the firm. How would this likely impact the supply of the manufactured good?
answers: There will be a decrease in supply
There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
explanation: A higher minimum wage raises the cost of production, shifting the whole supply curve left — a decrease in supply.

title: Supply of oil
questionText: Suppose that new fracking technology opens up new oil reserves. How would this likely impact the supply of oil?
answers: There will be a decrease in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be an increase in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
explanation: New fracking technology and reserves lower extraction costs and expand capacity, shifting supply right — an increase.

questionText: In the quest to reduce global CO2 emissions, more firms enter the mining sector to extract lithium for battery production. How would this affect the supply of lithium on global markets?
answers: There will be a decrease in supply
There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
explanation: More producers entering the market shifts the whole supply curve right — an increase in supply.

questionText: The cost of fertiliser purchased and used by the agricultural industry falls, increasing the supply of crops. Which factor best explains this shift?
answers: A fall in the price of crops
The provision of a subsidy
Improvement in technology
A decrease in the cost of factors of production
explanation: Fertiliser is an input, so cheaper fertiliser is a fall in the cost of the factors of production, which increases supply.

questionText: Suppose that an economy decides to subsidise its agricultural sector by giving payments to farmers who produce beef. How would this likely affect the supply of beef?
answers: There will be a decrease in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' effective costs, shifting the supply curve right — an increase in supply.

questionText: Which of the following changes would increase the supply of a good?
answers: An improvement in production technology
A decrease in the productivity of labour
A rise in the price of raw materials
A reduction in the size of the workforce
explanation: Better production technology lowers unit costs and raises output, increasing supply. The other options all reduce supply.

questionText: Consider the table below which shows changes to the tax placed on cigarettes. How would this likely impact the supply of cigarettes in year 2?
answers: There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
There will be a decrease in supply
explanation: A higher tax raises producers' costs, shifting supply left — a decrease in supply.

title: Supply of bananas
questionText: Suppose that a tropical cyclone damages the banana crop of an economy. What is the likely impact on supply?
answers: There will be a decrease in supply
There will be an increase in supply
There will be an expansion in supply
There will be a contraction in supply
explanation: Destroying part of the crop reduces what can be produced, shifting supply left — a decrease.

title: Supply of solar panels
questionText: An improvement in manufacturing technology shifts the supply of solar panels from S1 to S2. At a price of $600, by how much has the supply of solar panels increased?
answers: By 50 panels
By 100 panels
By 150 panels
By 200 panels
explanation: Read the horizontal gap between S1 and S2 at $600: quantity supplied rises by 100 panels.

title: Supply of steel
questionText: A sharp rise in the cost of iron ore shifts the supply of steel from S1 to S2. At a price of $600 per tonne, by how much has the supply of steel decreased?
answers: By 60 tonnes
By 90 tonnes
By 150 tonnes
By 120 tonnes
explanation: A dearer input (iron ore) shifts steel supply left. Reading the gap at $600 per tonne, quantity supplied falls by 120 tonnes.

title: Supply of milk
questionText: A government subsidy shifts the supply of milk from S1 to S2. At a price of $2 per litre, what quantity is now supplied, and how should the change be described?
answers: 160 litres, an increase of 160
320 litres, an increase of 160
320 litres, an expansion of 160
160 litres, an expansion of 160
explanation: The subsidy shifts supply right — an increase (a shift), not an expansion. At $2, S2 gives 320 litres, up 160 from 160.

title: Supply of tea
questionText: Which of the following factors could explain the shift in the supply of tea from S1 to S2?
answers: An increase in land rents on tea plantations
Selective breeding resulting in disease resistant tea plants
A decrease in the price of tea
An increase in the number of tea plantations
explanation: The leftward shift is a decrease in supply, caused by higher costs — an increase in land rents. The other options would raise supply or move along the curve.

title: Supply of petrol cars
questionText: What could explain the change in the supply of petrol cars from S1 to S2?
answers: The introduction of a tax on petrol cars
A rise in the wages of car factory workers
Increased use of robotics in the production of petrol cars
An increase in consumer demand for petrol cars
explanation: The rightward shift is an increase in supply from lower production costs — robotics. A tax or higher wages would decrease supply, and higher demand shifts demand, not supply.

questionText: Smartphones and tablets are substitutes in production: a contract manufacturer can assemble either on the same line, using the same workers and many of the same components. A surge in demand pushes the price of smartphones up sharply, while the price of tablets is unchanged. What happens to the supply of tablets?
answers: A contraction in supply, as producers move along the tablet supply curve
A decrease in supply, as the tablet supply curve shifts to the left
An increase in supply, as the tablet supply curve shifts to the right
No change in supply, because the price of tablets has not changed
explanation: Tablets and phones are substitutes in production. With phones now more profitable, the manufacturer switches its line to phones, shifting tablet supply left — a decrease.

questionText: Finished tablets can be held in warehouses and released at any time. Manufacturers now expect the price of tablets to fall sharply next quarter, when a new model launches. What is the most likely effect on the supply of tablets this quarter?
answers: A decrease in supply, as manufacturers hold stock back to sell next quarter
An expansion in supply, as producers move along the tablet supply curve
An increase in supply, as manufacturers release stock ahead of the price fall
No change in supply, because the price of tablets has not actually fallen yet
explanation: Expecting a price fall next quarter, producers release stored stock now to sell before prices drop, increasing current supply.

title: Supply of mobile phones
questionText: Suppose that the price of mobile phones fell by 20%. Given the curve shown, what would be the result in the supply of mobile phones?
answers: A decrease in supply of 40 mobile phones
An expansion in supply of 40 mobile phones
An increase in supply of 40 mobile phones
A contraction in supply of 40 mobile phones
explanation: A fall in the good's own price is a movement along the curve. Lower price makes production less profitable, so quantity supplied contracts by 40.
